lessons.title: Site and soil preparation
lessons.html:
Site and soil preparation

An orchard or vineyard stays in the ground for 15 to 30 years or more. Mistakes made at establishment are expensive and hard to fix later, so the foreman must understand each step and make sure it is done properly.

Choosing the site

  • Climate: enough winter chilling for deciduous fruit, low frost risk at flowering, and suitable summer temperatures.
  • Slope and aspect: cold air flows down slopes and collects in low spots (frost pockets). Aspect affects sun exposure.
  • Water: a legal, reliable irrigation water supply under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.
  • Access: roads for tractors, bins and trucks.

Soil survey

A soil scientist digs profile pits across the block to check depth, texture, stoniness, drainage, impermeable layers and chemistry. Soil samples are sent to a laboratory for pH, nutrients and salinity. The results guide soil preparation, fertiliser, rootstock choice and where to plant.

Soil preparation

Soil preparation is often done in the year before planting:

  1. Remove old trees or vines and their roots; this reduces root diseases and replant problems.
  2. Deep rip or delve to break compacted or hard layers, along the planned rows.
  3. Incorporate lime or gypsum where the soil analysis shows it is needed, mixing it into the root zone.
  4. Install drainage where water stands.
  5. Form ridges where drainage is poor, to keep roots out of waterlogged soil.

Erosion control

Plan rows, roads and waterways so that runoff does not cause erosion, in line with the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983. Cover crops between rows help to protect soil.

lessons.title: Planning the block and planting
lessons.html:
Planning the block and planting

Cultivar and rootstock

The farm manager and consultant choose cultivars for market demand and climate, rootstocks for soil and vigour, and pollinator cultivars where needed. Plants should be certified, disease-free nursery material from registered nurseries. Check plants on arrival: correct labels, healthy roots, no damage, no pests.

Layout

  • Row direction: often north-south for even light on both sides, adjusted to the slope.
  • Spacing: row width allows tractors and sprayers to pass; in-row spacing depends on rootstock vigour and training system.
  • Trellis: vines and many intensive orchards need a trellis of posts, anchors and wires, ideally installed before or at planting.
  • Irrigation: drip or micro-irrigation installed and tested before planting.
  • Windbreaks where wind damage is a risk.

Marking out

Mark rows and plant positions accurately using a survey, GPS or measured lines. Straight rows make every future job easier.

Planting

  1. Keep plants cool and roots moist until planting; never let roots dry in the sun.
  2. Trim damaged roots as instructed.
  3. Plant at the same depth as in the nursery, with the graft union well above the soil.
  4. Firm the soil around roots to remove air pockets.
  5. Irrigate immediately after planting.
  6. Cut back the plant to the height the training system requires.
  7. Protect young trunks from sunburn (white paint) and from rabbits or other animals where needed.

Supervising planting teams

Check a sample of planted trees per row for depth, firmness, graft height and straightness. Correct mistakes immediately. Record the cultivar, rootstock, number planted and date per block.

lessons.title: Caring for young plants
lessons.html:
Caring for young plants

The first years

The aim in the first one to three years is to build a strong root system and the framework of the tree or vine, not to carry a crop. Allowing young plants to bear fruit too early can stunt them.

Irrigation

Young plants have small root systems and dry out quickly. Irrigate little and often, and check that every dripper or emitter is working and placed near the plant. Check soil moisture with a spade or probes. Avoid waterlogging.

Weed control

Weeds compete strongly with young plants for water and nutrients. Keep a weed-free strip along the row by hand hoeing, mulch or herbicides used according to the label. Never let herbicide spray drift onto the green bark or leaves of young plants; use shields.

Fertilising

Apply small amounts of fertiliser as recommended by soil analysis and the consultant, spread around the root zone, not against the trunk.

Training

Train the young tree or vine to the chosen system: select and tie main branches or the trunk and cordon, remove unwanted shoots, and attach to the trellis or stake with ties that will not cut into the bark. Check ties regularly.

Pest and disease watch

Young leaves attract aphids, mites, leafroller caterpillars and fungal diseases. Scout regularly and report. Replace dead plants in the next planting window and record replacements.

Records

RecordUse

Planting date and numbersAge and stand counts

Irrigation and fertiliserGrowth follow-up

Key points

  • Choose the site carefully for climate, slope, water and access.
  • Use a soil survey to guide soil preparation and rootstock choice.
  • Prepare the soil and install trellis and irrigation before planting.
  • Plant at nursery depth with the graft union above the soil and irrigate immediately.
  • In early years, build roots and framework, not crop.

quiz.question: Why should low spots on a slope be avoided for fruit trees?

options.text: They are frost pockets where cold air collects

quiz.question: What is the purpose of soil profile pits before planting?

options.text: To check soil depth, texture, drainage and hard layers

quiz.question: How deep should a young grafted tree be planted?

options.text: At nursery depth with the graft union above the soil

quiz.question: What should be done immediately after planting?

options.text: Apply a heavy fertiliser dose against the trunk

quiz.question: Why is cropping very young trees discouraged?

options.text: The fruit is illegal to sell

quiz.question: Nursery plant roots can be left in the sun for a day before planting without harm.
